problem_statement: In a 9-node RPL+TSCH+Orchestra network (built with Orchestra enabled and RPL storing-mode routing), the DAG root does not converge its route table: it never manages to install routes covering the entire network. A scenario that waits for the root to advertise 'Routing entries: 8' (i.e., a route to every other node) times out without that condition being met, so the network cannot be treated as fully reachable even though all nodes are in radio range. The same symptom appears when the network is driven by the existing receiver- and sender-based unicast scheduling rules as well as by the new link-based unicast scheduling rule; in each case the root's routing table is left incomplete and reachability to all nodes is not achieved.
causal_chain: Both upstream Cooja scenarios build the same simple-node application with Orchestra active and assert, via the LogListener/ScriptRunner, that the root node (ID:1) eventually prints 'Routing entries: 8' and then call log.testOK(). Before the fix this condition is never reached within the 6-minute timeout, so the scenario fails; after the production change it is reached and the scenario passes. The assertion depends on TSCH schedule behavior: the production change adds a parameter to tsch_schedule_add_link controlling whether an existing link at the same timeslot/channel is first removed, changes tsch_schedule_remove_link_by_timeslot to clear every matching link (not just one) when the schedule is unlocked, and introduces a new link-based unicast rule whose add/remove path deliberately skips the old-link removal (passing do_remove=0) so that a transmit and receive cell can coexist at the same timeslot on the same channel. The link-based rule also needs a two-address hash to derive timeslot/channel for a node pair. These changes let the unicast cells and the resulting neighbor routes build up correctly so that the root's route table fills to 8 entries, flipping the scenario from fail to pass. The recorded fail-to-pass set is exactly these two scenarios, with no pass-to-pass cases.
